finding.claim: Broken authorization on project deletion: the DELETE handler calls authorized(), which returns a boolean, and discards the result. It never throws, so any authenticated user can delete any project. The sibling PUT handler correctly uses authorize(), which throws a 403. This is a near-duplicate with a meaningful difference.
finding.source: Any authenticated user sends DELETE /projects/:id with an id of a project they do not own.

trace.note: DELETE /projects/:id handler is entered by any authenticated user
Project is fetched by the attacker-supplied id; there is no ownership filter
authorized(req.user, project) returns false for a non-owner, but the return value is ignored and nothing is thrown

finding.guards_checked: authorize() at api.js:4 throws on a non-owner who is not an admin, but the DELETE route does not call it. authorized() at api.js:12 only returns a boolean. This is the only file in the repository, so there is no auth middleware that could compensate. req.user is assumed to be set upstream. The route also does not handle a missing project, where get() may return undefined. That is a robustness issue and not a security finding.

verdict.guard_found: authorized() at api.js:12 returns a boolean and is discarded at api.js:18; authorize() at api.js:4 throws but is only called in the PUT route (api.js:25). No middleware exists in this file.
verdict.reason: api.js:18 calls authorized(req.user, project) as a bare statement, so its boolean is ignored, and api.js:19 deletes the project unconditionally, which lets any authenticated non-owner delete it; the PUT route at api.js:25 uses the throwing authorize().
